title: Anti-Pattern: Document Structure Failures
body:
# Anti-Pattern: Document Structure Failures

Structural failures are document-level defects that the qa-coherence agent catches. They are distinct from prose-level failures (voice, claims) — a document can be beautifully written at the sentence level and still fail structurally. The outline-architect's job is to prevent structural failures before drafting. The qa-coherence agent catches what slipped through.

---

## Pattern 1: Orphaned Points

**Definition:** An idea is introduced — in the intro, a section heading, a transitional sentence — but is never developed. The reader expects a payoff that never arrives.

**Why it fails the reader:** The reader stores the introduced idea as a pending question. When the payoff never comes, the reader either re-reads looking for the missed content or finishes with a persistent sense that something was omitted. Both outcomes are failures.

**Detection method:** For every claim in the introduction, check that a section delivers on it. For every section heading, check that the section body addresses the title directly. For every "we will examine" or "as discussed below" reference, check that the examination or discussion exists.

**Correction:** Either develop the orphaned point where it belongs, or remove its introduction from wherever it was announced.

---

## Pattern 2: Section Bloat

**Definition:** One section contains two or more logically distinct sub-topics that each deserve their own scope declaration. The section does the work of multiple sections without acknowledging it.

**Why it fails the reader:** The reader cannot form a clear mental model of what the section is about. When sections have multiple purposes, QA cannot evaluate whether either purpose was served. The outline does not give section-drafter a clear scope.

**Detection method:** Can you write a single-sentence purpose statement for this section? If the purpose statement requires "and also," the section is bloated.

**Correction:** Split into two sections, each with its own scope declaration. Update the word count allocation. The merge-normalizer must be informed of the split.

---

## Pattern 3: Preview-and-Recap Loops

**Definition:** The introduction tells the reader what the document will cover. Each section begins by restating what the prior section covered. The conclusion restates what all sections covered. No new value is added at any transition.

**Why it fails the reader:** The preview-recap loop is a word count multiplier that adds length without adding information. A document with a 200-word intro, 50-word section openers, and a 200-word conclusion that all say the same things has wasted 600+ words. The reader experience is: "I am being told what I am about to be told, then told it, then told what I was told."

**Detection method:** Read only the intro, all section-opening sentences, and the conclusion. If these alone tell the full story, the document has a preview-recap problem.

**Correction:** Introductions should pose the problem or question the document answers — not preview the sections. Section openers should start with the section's first claim — not summarize the prior section. Conclusions should advance the argument — not restate it.

---

## Pattern 4: Burying the Lead

**Definition:** The most important finding, recommendation, or conclusion appears late in the document — in section 4 of 5, or in the final paragraph.

**Why it fails the reader:** Most professional readers decide whether a document is useful within the first two paragraphs. If the key finding is buried, most readers who needed that finding will have stopped reading before they reached it.

**Detection method:** What is the single most important claim in this document? Where does it appear?

**Correction:** Apply bottom-line-up-front. The most important claim belongs in the first section, not the last. Background and rationale follow, not precede, the conclusion. This applies to all internal documents and most general documents. Exception: documents structured as arguments that build to a conclusion may hold the claim — but only if the structure is intentional and the reader will stay for the argument.

---

## Pattern 5: Generic Section Names

**Definition:** Section titles that describe the section's category rather than its specific content: "Background," "Overview," "Introduction," "Analysis," "Discussion," "Conclusion."

**Why it fails the reader:** Generic section names provide no information about what the section contains. A reader scanning headings cannot determine whether to read a section called "Background" — they can determine whether to read a section called "Why Traditional Recommendation Approaches Break at Scale."

**Detection method:** Could this section title appear in any document on any topic? If yes, it is too generic.

**Correction:** Replace with a title specific to this document's argument. The title should be specific enough that a section-drafter knows what to write without reading the scope notes.

---

## Pattern 6: Scope Creep Within Sections

**Definition:** A section expands beyond its declared scope to cover material that belongs in another section — or nowhere in the document.

**Detection method:** Compare the section content against the scope_notes in the outline. Check whether any content in this section was explicitly declared out of scope.

**Correction:** Move out-of-scope content to the appropriate section, or cut it if it belongs nowhere. Inform merge-normalizer of the moved content so the receiving section can be reassessed.

---

## Pattern 7: Missing Transitions

**Definition:** Sections or paragraphs follow each other without any logical connection established between them. The reader must infer the relationship.

**Why it fails the reader:** "Structure is an argument" (Editorial Doctrine Rule 4). When sections follow each other without connection, the reader cannot understand why the document is ordered the way it is. The argument collapses.

**Detection method:** At each section boundary, ask: what does the reader know at the end of section N that makes section N+1 useful? If you cannot answer this, the transition is missing.

**Correction:** Write one transition sentence at the end of section N or the beginning of section N+1 that names the specific logical connection. The transition should not be generic — it should name the specific concept being carried forward.
